title: How do we write eight thirds as a mixed number?
description: Eight thirds is split into the thirds that make whole units and the thirds that are left. The board writes it as a whole number plus a fraction and then reads and writes it as a mixed number. Keeko doubts that the leftover thirds count as a whole.
teaching_notes: One idea: take out as many groups of the bottom number as possible; the whole number counts the groups and the fraction holds the rest. Watch for students who round the leftover up to another whole.

source: Write 8/3 as a whole number plus a fraction, and say how it is read and written as a mixed number.
video_script.why: A learner writes a fraction greater than one as a whole number plus a fraction and reads it as a mixed number.
video_script.substitution: the book's own fraction eight thirds
video_script.anchor: eight third-unit bars on a number line from 0 to 3
video_script.wrong_answer: eight thirds has three wholes, because the leftover two thirds also count
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko rounds the leftover up to a whole, though two thirds cannot fill a unit that needs three thirds.
video_script.payoff_line: Eight thirds is two plus two thirds

final_answer.spoken: eight thirds is two plus two thirds, read two and two thirds

video_script.fraction_reading: one third, two thirds, six thirds, eight thirds
maths_rules: 3 thirds make 1 whole, so 6 thirds make 2 wholes
read 'two and two thirds' and written 2 2/3, a mixed number
video_script.design: Eight third bars laid from zero. They join in threes into two whole bars and two thirds are left.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; a number line from 0 to 3 with each unit cut into three parts; the black line of 8/3 from 0

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.line: the number line appears with each unit cut into three equal parts
marks.black: the black line of eight thirds is drawn from zero and passes the mark two

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book, and it uses a number line.
<bookmark mark='line'/>Each unit on this number line is cut into three equal parts.
<bookmark mark='black'/>The black line is eight thirds long.
How can we write eight thirds as a whole number plus a fraction?

beats.on_screen: the number line and the black line stay; the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: eight third bars in a row from 0; a whole unit bar as long as three third bars; the words mixed number beside a whole number and a fraction

marks.bars: eight third bars of equal size line up from zero
marks.whole: a whole unit bar is shown beside them, as long as three third bars
marks.mixed: a whole number and a fraction are written side by side and labelled mixed number

narration: <bookmark mark='bars'/>Eight thirds means eight parts, and each part is one third of a unit.
<bookmark mark='whole'/>A whole unit is the same length as three of those thirds.
<bookmark mark='mixed'/>A whole number and a fraction written together is called a mixed number.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the fraction that we have to look at is eight thirds.

beats.on_screen: To find: 8/3 as a whole number plus a fraction, and as a mixed number
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to write it as a whole number plus a fraction, and then as a mixed number.

marks.split: the eight third bars are split into a group of six and a group of two

beats.colours: group of six = one colour, group of two = second colour
narration: <bookmark mark='split'/>Step one, split eight thirds into six thirds and two thirds. Six is the biggest number of thirds that makes whole units.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 3 thirds make 1 whole, so 6 thirds make 2 wholes

marks.first: the first three third bars join into one whole unit bar
marks.second: the next three third bars join into a second whole unit bar

beats.colours: each group of three thirds = its own colour
narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step two, three thirds make one whole.
<bookmark mark='second'/>Six thirds make two wholes, because there are two groups of three thirds.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: put together the 2 wholes and the 2 thirds left

marks.sum: the two wholes and the two thirds are put together as a whole number and a fraction
marks.mixed: the whole number and the fraction are placed side by side

narration: <bookmark mark='sum'/>Step three, put together the two wholes and the two thirds that are left.
<bookmark mark='mixed'/>The whole number and the fraction sit side by side.

marks.check: the two wholes and the two left over thirds are put back together as eight thirds

narration: <bookmark mark='check'/>To check, put the pieces back together. Six thirds and two thirds make eight thirds again.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 8/3 = 2 + 2/3, read 'two and two thirds', written 2 2/3
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Eight thirds is two plus two thirds.
We read it as two and two thirds. Written this way, it is a mixed number.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the number line
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: a bubble says 8/3 has 3 wholes because the leftover 2 thirds also count; the 2 left over thirds are laid against a whole bar and fall short; the bubble is struck out

marks.doubt: the bubble with the wrong idea appears
marks.short: the two left over thirds are laid against a whole unit bar and stop one third short
marks.fix: the bubble is struck out and the leftover is kept as two thirds

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks eight thirds has three wholes, because the leftover two thirds also count.
<bookmark mark='short'/>Lay the two thirds against a whole unit. They stop one third short.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>A whole needs three thirds, so the leftover stays as a fraction.
